transcript:
>> This is "NPR News Now."
The latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from "NPR News" in
Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Political parties are spending
heavily in dozens of House races.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reports
they're investing six-figure
sums in advertising in 70
districts.
>> Spending data from Ad Impact
suggests the question is less
about whether there will be a
Democratic wave in the House,
but rather how high it could
crest.
Several races will see more than
$10 million in ads between now
and Tuesday, including toss-up
races in Michigan, North
Carolina, New York, and Florida.
Seven-figure ad buys in very
conservative communities in
Tennessee, Oklahoma, and
Arkansas, and last-minute
resources to districts where
gerrymandering by Republicans
could backfire.
These 70 districts voted for
Trump by an average of nine
points in 2024, highlighting the
impact of the Trump
administration's unpopularity
with voters over the last year.
Steven Fowler, NPR News, Atlanta.
>> The federal government has
appealed a court decision,
allowing California to count
ballots that the Trump
administration says were sent to
non-citizen voters.
The appeal came just hours after
a district judge rejected the
Justice Department's attempt to
segregate about 20,000 disputed
ballots.
The Justice Department insists
it's trying to prevent
fraudulent voting.
Millions of Californians have
already voted.
Opposition leader Maria Karina
Machado says Venezuela's
advance toward democracy is
irreversible, and PRS Carrie
Kahn reports she gave her first
public address today after her
surprise return to the country
last week.
>> Dressed in a white suit, her
trademark color, Machado think
President Trump for his support
and U.S.-backed plans to have
elections, which she said would
be in 2027.
>> [ Speaking Spanish ]
>> The Democratic transition is
irreversible and will be
peaceful, she said.
She criticized an opaque U.S.
brokered oil deal and said her
return was successful unlike
previous attempts because,
quote, "They didn't see it
coming."
Machado is now a direct
challenge to the U.S.-backed
interim president, Delcie
Rodriguez, who made her own
speech one hour before Machado's.
Rodriguez announced elections
were coming and dismissed the
opposition leader's return as a
quote, "show."
Carrie Kahn, NPR News,
Rio de Janeiro.
>> What if this curse at hand
were thicker than itself with
brother's blood?
Is there not rain enough in the
sweet heavens to wash it?
Why does it snow?
>> Patrick Stewart has died.
The classically-trained stage
actor was possibly best known
for the "Star Trek" franchise
and the "X-Men" films.
But Stewart was also an
accomplished stage actor who
joined the Royal Shakespeare
Company when he was 26 years
old and celebrated for his
interpretation of roles like
King Lear, Macbeth, and
Claudius.
A spokesperson says Stewart
died after, quote, "a brief and
poignant journey with Alzheimer's
disease and Lewy body dementia."
Patrick Stewart was 86 years old.
You're listening to NPR News
from Washington.
A state judge is set to consider
whether social media posts by
New York Attorney General
Letitia James should disqualify
her from leading a criminal
investigation into gang rape
allegations at Cornell
University.
One of the accused men wants
James removed as special
prosecutor claiming bias.
James' office argues the
challenge is without merit.
"Life" magazine is returning to
news stands next month as a
quarterly print publication,
and Piers Chloe Veltman reports
"Life" will also have videos,
online articles, and events.
>> Supermodel and entrepreneur
Karlie Kloss' Bedford Media
Company acquired "Life" in 2024.
It also bought "Legacy"
magazine's "ID&W."
In a 2025 episode of the Aspire
podcast, Kloss described her
acquisitions as "storied brands."
>> They mean things to people.
What they stand for,
what the role they've played in
sort of pop culture or culture,
and that is a very hard thing to
manufacture or build from the
ground up.
>> Time magazine publisher
Henry Luce launched "Life" as a
weekly in 1936.
Its boxy red logo became
synonymous with high-quality
photojournalism.
Since folding as a weekly in
1972, the magazine has come back
and fits and starts, most
recently until 2007 as a weekly
newspaper supplement.
Chloe Veltman, NPR News.
>> A renowned oceanographer is
urging an end to krill fishing
near Antarctica as the U.S.,
China, and Russia try to expand
the practice.
Sylvia Earle says there's no
sustainable way to harvest krill
without harming whales that feed
on the tiny crustaceans.
Krill are harvested for fish
feed and omega-3 supplements.
This is "NPR News" from
Washington.

topics.text: Political parties spending heavily in 70 House districts, with over $10 million in some races
Federal government appeals California ruling allowing counting of disputed ballots sent to non-citizens
Venezuela opposition leader Maria Corina Machado makes first public address after return, calls transition irreversible
Actor Patrick Stewart dies at 86 after Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia
State judge to consider whether Attorney General Letitia James should be disqualified from Cornell gang rape investigation
Life magazine returns to newsstands next month as a quarterly print publication under Karlie Kloss's company
Oceanographer Sylvia Earle urges end to Antarctic krill fishing, citing harm to whales
